questions.question: For one roll of an ordinary six-sided die, the sample space S is:
options: The set of even numbers only

questions.question: An event with probability 1 is:
A learner's working produces a probability of $1{,}4$. The correct conclusion is:
options: The answer should be rounded to 1
The event happens 1,4 times per trial
The calculation is wrong — every probability lies between 0 and 1

questions.question: The theoretical probability formula $P(E) = \dfrac{n(E)}{n(S)}$ may only be used when:
options: All outcomes in the sample space are equally likely
The experiment has been repeated many times
The event has more than one outcome

questions.question: The probability of rolling a number greater than 4 on a fair die is:
A bag holds 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters. $P(\text{blue})$ is:
options: $\dfrac{3}{10}$ — three blue counters out of ten counters

questions.question: From the same bag, $P(\text{red or green})$ is:
A bottle top lands cap-up 120 times in 200 flips. The relative frequency of cap-up is:
options: $0{,}5$ — two outcomes are always equally likely

questions.question: Relative frequency must be used for the bottle top because:
options: Bottle tops have more than two outcomes
The formula $\dfrac{n(E)}{n(S)}$ gives a number above 1 here
Its outcomes are not equally likely, so theoretical counting does not apply
Experiments are always more accurate than theory

questions.question: A fair coin shows 27 heads in 50 flips (relative frequency 0,54). The best conclusion is:
options: The coin is biased toward heads
The theoretical probability of heads is now 0,54
Normal small-sample variation — with more flips the relative frequency should settle near 0,5

questions.question: As the number of trials grows very large, the relative frequency of an event:
options: Settles ever closer to the true (theoretical) probability

questions.question: The complement of the event 'rolling a 6' on a die is:
If the probability of rain tomorrow is 0,3, the probability of NO rain is:
options: It cannot be found from the given information

questions.question: $P(A) + P(\text{not } A) = 1$ holds because A and its complement are:
options: Mutually exclusive AND exhaustive — they cannot both happen, but one must

questions.question: For the bag of 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters, $P(\text{not green})$ is:

subtopics.title: A Scale From Impossible to Certain

questions.question: On the washing line from 0 to 1, the event 'a fair die shows an even number' pegs at:
options: Just left of the right pole

questions.question: The event 'a die shows 7' pegs at 0 because:
options: The sample space contains no 7 — the event is impossible
The die must be rolled twice to reach 7

questions.question: The washing line works as an error detector because:
options: It shows which events are most common
No valid probability can peg left of 0 or right of 1, so answers outside that range are wrong

subtopics.title: Counting Your Way to a Probability

questions.question: The two questions of the counting engine are:
options: How many could happen, and how many of those make the event — then divide
How many trials, and how long they took
What is the biggest and smallest outcome

questions.question: For the packet of 10 sweets with 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green, the trap answer 'a third for blue' fails because:
options: The correct answer is a half
The equal candidates are the 10 sweets, not the 3 colours — each red has its own chance

questions.question: The probability of drawing red or green from that packet is:
Five flips of a bottle top give 4 cap-ups. Treating 0,8 as the true probability is unwise because:
options: Bottle tops change shape as they are flipped
The relative frequency should be multiplied by 2
Five trials is far too small a sample — short runs wobble; the estimate needs many more flips

questions.question: Which object REQUIRES the experience engine (relative frequency) rather than counting?
options: A lopsided drawing pin landing point-up or point-down
A shaken bag of identical counters

questions.question: A coin shows 1 400 heads in 2 000 flips (relative frequency 0,7). The reasonable verdict is:
options: The coin is very likely biased — a large sample should not sit that far from 0,5
Normal wobble; flip five more times
The theoretical probability of heads was always 0,7
Heads is simply luckier than tails
